catalog_quote: [Published chapter p. 449] Nkoroo is a two-tone plus downstep language. The examples in (1) illustrate this lexical contrast. (1) Tonal contrast in Nkoroo: ókí (HH) 'take', ó↓kí (H↓H) 'swim', ókì (HL) 'swordfish'. ... the overall pitch pattern in nominal compounds shows that Nkoroo may be moving in the direction of an accentual system, with fixed tonal melodies associated with particular morpho-syntactic categories. Other scholars, including Jenewari (1977) and Williamson (1978, 1986) have made similar “accentual” observations about Ijoid languages in general, and Harry (1987) has made this observation about Nkoroo. [p. 447, abstract] The language calls for a fixed melody, HL, in noun compounds and pro-clitic+noun host combinations, except when the first noun is L-toned. Nkoroo phrases on the other hand have no fixed surface pitch patterns. [pp. 464-465, Conclusion] Nkoroo noun compounds and pro-clitic+noun host combinations share a fixed tone pattern: they take a uniform HL pattern, except the noun is L-toned. In this case the entire compound is L. This output tone occurs without regard to the input tone of the noun. ... The overall pattern shows the gradual movement in the direction of an accentual system, which is now widespread in Ijoid (Williamson 1978).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nkoroo is described as a two-tone (H, L) plus downstep language whose lexical prosody is tonal; no word stress is described or mentioned. The authors add that Nkoroo is drifting toward an 'accentual' system in the Ijoid sense: nouns keep their lexical tone in isolation and in most phrases, but compounds, proclitic+noun and 'one'+noun units neutralise input tones to a single culminative HL contour (fall after the first syllable of the second element), or all-L when the first element/clitic is L. Whether a syllable is 'stressed' is never at issue.
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal: no HLHL compounds ('If the fall already occurs on the first noun, there cannot be a second fall on the second noun', p. 2); voiceless consonants block H spreading in demonstrative+noun (p. 9); numerals 2-4 and 'some/many' leave the noun's underlying tone unaffected; numerals 5-9 carry a L clitic [a] whose L spreads to the noun's first syllable (p. 8).
new_statements.domain_note: Word- and phrase-level tone of nouns in isolation, noun+noun compounds, proclitic+noun, numeral+noun and demonstrative+noun; data from the NSF documentation project in Nkoroo town (2007-2011). Sentence prosody only via Harry (1987: 72), quoted in the ACAL 40 slides: questions and statements have the same pitch patterns.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes the Nkoroo of Nkoroo town (Opobo/Nkoroo LGA, Rivers State), i.e. nkor1239 itself, which Obikudo (2024: 2509) says 'is referred to as Kirika by its speakers'; Glottolog lists no dialects. It is an Eastern Ijo variety (closest relatives Kalabari, Ibani, Kirike/Okrika) and is the daily language of the Defaka [defa1248] community, whose phonetics Shryock et al. say may be indistinguishable from Nkoroo at that level; Akinlabi & Connell argue the two tone systems remain distinct.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the published version of the WOCAL 6 handout already recorded as the existing statement (Akinlabi & Connell 2009: 'two-tone plus downstep', Nkoroo 'moved in the direction of an accentual system'). Same claims, same reading (tone language, no stress statement); it adds the page-numbered published source and the explicit attribution of the accentual observation to Harry (1987), Jenewari (1977) and Williamson (1978, 1986). The catalog record for Nkoroo has an empty rule, so this supports keeping it as tonal/no-stress rather than filling a stress placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nkoroo is a register tone language with two level tones (H, L) plus downstep, lexically contrastive (oki HH 'take' vs H!H 'swim' vs HL 'swordfish'). Noun+noun compounds and proclitic+host combinations take a fixed HL melody (all-L when the head noun is L-toned) regardless of input tones; phrases keep their lexical tones. The authors interpret the fixed compound melody as a drift toward an 'accentual' (pitch accent-like) system in the sense of Williamson 1978, but the paper contains no statement about word stress and no stress placement.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds and proclitic+noun combinations whose (first/head) noun is L-toned surface all-L instead of HL (p. 447, p. 464). No stress exceptions, since no stress rule is given.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern Nkoroo/Nkọrọọ of Nkoroo town (Opobo/Nkoroo LGA, Rivers State, Nigeria), self-name Kirika, classified as an Eastern Ijoid lect alongside Kalabari, Ibani and Okrika; the Festschrift paper notes Kirika is not Okrika. Defaka (defa1248), spoken in the same town, is a separate language treated in the WOCAL 6 handout but not in the works read here.

new_statements.quote: 3.2. Tone. Like the other Eastern Ijoid lects, Nkoroo operates a register tone system made up of two level tones, a high [ˊ] and a low [ˋ] plus a downstepped high [ǃ]. In the Ijoid orthography, the low tone is left unmarked, while the downstepped high is marked with a macron ( n ). In this paper, all tones and sound segments are represented phonetically using IPA symbols.
